title: Epistles
subtitle: Selected letters of spiritual counsel
source: Editorial framing summarizes the contents and themes of Elder Paisios's letters to the nuns of Souroti and to other spiritual children, the originals of which were published in Greek by the Holy Monastery of St. John the Theologian and remain under copyright. Brief quoted sentences below are widely reported in the Elder's oral tradition. For the full text the reader is directed to the printed Epistles in their authorized translations.

sections.title: To a Disciple Discouraged in the Struggle
sections.framing: Among the recurring counsels in the Elder's correspondence is the assurance to disciples weighed down by the slowness of their progress that God measures the struggle, not the result. He told them that the falls of a soul who is fighting are not the same as the falls of a soul who has given up, and that the very awareness of one's faults is itself a gift of God's grace. He urged frequent confession, the keeping of small rules faithfully, and a refusal to compare one's interior life to anyone else's.
paragraphs: Do not look at how far you are from where you want to be. Look at the road, and walk it one step at a time. God is not in a hurry.
notes: The Elder's counsel here echoes St. John Climacus, whose Ladder he commended to every serious Christian.

sections.title: On Prayer for Those Who Have Strayed
sections.framing: Many of the Elder's letters are answers to parents grieving over children who had abandoned the Church or fallen into ruinous lives. He directed such parents away from arguments and reproaches and toward prayer of a particular kind: prayer joined to fasting, almsgiving in the child's name, and patient love that does not cease. The mother's tears for her child, he wrote, are never lost; the child does not see them, but God collects them.
paragraphs: Pray for your child without complaining to him. Words wound; prayer heals. Let God speak to his heart in His own time.
notes: Compare St. Monica, whose tears for Augustine the Elder occasionally invoked when writing to mothers.

sections.title: On Joy in the Cell
sections.framing: Writing to nuns and to lay disciples who lived in difficult circumstances, the Elder insisted that joy is a sign of the Holy Spirit and the natural fruit of a clear conscience. He distinguished it from the cheerfulness of distraction. Christian joy, he said, can sit beside sorrow, and even sing in prison; gloom in a Christian is a symptom of self-love that has been wounded.
paragraphs: If you love Christ, you will not be able to keep silent for joy. Joy is the perfume that the Spirit leaves wherever He passes.
notes: St. Seraphim of Sarov's greeting, "Christ is risen, my joy!" was a refrain the Elder often quoted to his visitors.
